title: Where does each kind of data live so the site stays static and the platform stays cheap?
summary: The brief wants static/file-based infrastructure wherever practical and dynamic state where necessary. Evaluate pure static, database-backed, hybrid, JSONL event logs + compaction + published snapshots, and Workers combining static and dynamic on the brief's 19 criteria. Include the right-to-erasure tension with append-only logs.

title: Money (the ledger) needs its own dedicated research; a JSONL or DO log is not a source of truth for funds
summary: No payments code exists in this repo yet, and a sibling research topic (research/payments) is presumably covering this in depth. The one thing worth stating here: whatever the ledger design, the real source of truth for money movement is the payment processor (Stripe or similar), and any local ledger table is a reconciled mirror, never itself authoritative -- the opposite of every other category in question 1, where this site is the source of truth.

title: (B) D1-centric CRUD: simplest mental model for writes, but no coordination and now has global read replicas
summary: D1 in 2026 has global read replication across 6 regions via the Sessions API with sequential consistency (read-your-writes, monotonic reads), at no extra billing -- so the old objection that D1 is single-region for reads is weaker than it was. The remaining gap is coordination: two Workers can race a read-modify-write on one row with nothing serializing them, unlike a DO. Good fit for identity, likes, and any row-shaped read-heavy data; wrong fit for a live chat room.

title: (D) R2 JSONL event logs plus compaction Worker plus static snapshots: cheapest storage, no live coordination
summary: R2 storage is 0.015 dollars per GB-month with free egress, so it is by far the cheapest place to keep a growing log, and reading a compacted static snapshot from R2 through the Worker assets binding costs nothing extra at the edge once cached. What it does not give you is a writer with ordering: R2 has no equivalent of a DO's single-threaded queue, so two Workers appending to the same key can race -- this architecture wants a single Queue consumer as the one writer, which is really (C) with the sequencer moved into a Queue instead of a DO.

title: Crypto-shredding does not cleanly satisfy GDPR erasure against an append-only log, and specialists say so directly
summary: The standard mitigation -- encrypt personal fields per-subject, delete the key, leave the ciphertext in the log forever -- is argued by more than one source to still count as holding personal data under GDPR, because encrypted personal data is still personal data whether or not anyone holds the key. Practical write-ups converge on a mixed answer instead: short retention for anything sensitive, crypto-shredding only as a second layer, and a separate forgettable-payload store for fields that must actually vanish on request.

title: GitHub REST API caps authenticated writes at 5000 requests per hour, 60 for anonymous
summary: Fetched 2026-09-04 from GitHub's rate-limit docs. A personal access token or OAuth token gets 5000 requests per hour; a GitHub App installation gets the same floor, scaling up only with users and repos, capped at 12500/hour even then. Committing every chat message or like individually through the API is off the table at any real traffic before this ceiling is even considered.

title: GitHub also enforces a separate, tighter secondary limit on content-creating requests: 80 per minute, 500 per hour
summary: Fetched 2026-09-04. This secondary limit applies to content-generating actions (creating commits, files, issues) across REST, GraphQL, and the web UI combined, and GitHub also recommends no more than 6 pushes per minute per repository. This is the number that actually rules out git-as-a-live-write-path -- far tighter than the 5000/hour headline figure.

title: GitHub recommends repositories stay under 1GB, and will intervene past 5GB
summary: Fetched 2026-09-04, from GitHub's repository-limits docs plus corroborating community threads. There is no single hard cap, but GitHub Support recommends keeping a repo under 1GB for good performance and says a repo over 5GB may get a request to trim it. Every commit is a permanent blob; a JSONL log of daily activity committed forever, never squashed, is the fastest way to hit that boundary.

title: R2 plus a Worker is the better default compaction target; git is the fallback for content someone should review
summary: R2 has no rate ceiling remotely resembling GitHub's, Class A (write) operations are 4.50 dollars per million, and a Worker in front of it can serve the compacted snapshot at the edge for close to nothing once cached (question 5). Git-committing should be reserved for the subset of compacted history that has editorial value and deserves a diff and a revert -- a monthly digest, not every day's raw chat log.

title: Workers can route by path in one script: run_worker_first as a pattern array sends /api/* to code, everything else to static assets first
summary: Fetched 2026-09-04. The assets binding defaults to serving a matching static file before the Worker ever runs; setting run_worker_first (a boolean or a path-pattern array) lets one Worker handle specific routes like /api/* unconditionally while every other request stays asset-first. This is the concrete mechanism for question 5's Worker-layer merge -- one deployable, one script, no separate origin.

title: D1 rows_read bills scanned rows, not returned rows -- an unindexed query is charged for the whole table on every call
summary: Fetched 2026-09-04 from Cloudflare's own indexing guidance: rows read measures how many rows a query scans regardless of how many it returns, and D1's dashboard exposes meta.rows_read per query specifically to catch this. Adding an index so D1 can jump straight to the needed rows is the documented fix -- this is the mechanism behind the next entry's real bill.

title: A real D1 bill hit 127.6 billion row reads from four unindexed queries on a 765000-row table before indexes cut it 95 percent
summary: Published 2026-04-25, updated 2026-04-26. One select-max query alone scanned the full table on every page load, 765283 rows read per call, projecting to roughly 400 billion rows per month. Adding composite indexes plus ANALYZE brought that same query to 1 row read and the projected monthly total to about 19 billion rows, a 95 percent cut. Directly relevant to question 6: an Omnibox query without the right index is not a cost risk, it is a guaranteed one.

title: D1 rows read for a 20-post topic page: about 20-25 with a covering index, unbounded without one
summary: A query filtered and ordered by an index on (topic_id, published_at) LIMIT 20 should read close to the 20 rows it returns, plus a handful for the topic lookup itself -- call it 21-25 rows per page view. Without that index it becomes a full scan proportional to the whole posts table, the exact failure mode the prior D1-bill entry measured in production. This is a reasoned estimate, not a measurement against a live database -- worth checking against an actual EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN before shipping.

title: FTS5 full-text index overhead on D1 runs 20-30 percent of the base table size, per one practitioner benchmark
summary: Article dated 2025-03-17, fetched 2026-09-04. 500000 rows at roughly 800 words each store about 400MB of text; the FTS5 virtual table adds another 80-120MB on top, and the author advises budgeting 25 percent overhead per FTS5 table against D1's per-database storage cap. Single-term queries on that 500K-row index measured 8ms median, 22ms p99. This is one team's numbers, not a vendor-published figure, so it is a data point, not a guarantee.

title: Omnibox at 10000 topics and 1000000 posts: static index trivial, a full-body FTS5 index would blow the D1 free tier
summary: A static topics-plus-pages index entry (title, url, a few tags) measures under 150 bytes as JSON; 10000 of them is under 1.5MB, servable as one deploy-time file with no server. For 1000000 posts, indexing full body text with FTS5 at the prior entry's 20-30 percent overhead ratio would land in the hundreds of MB to low GB depending on post length -- fine on the 10GB Workers Paid cap, impossible on the 500MB Free plan. Indexing only title, tags, and a short excerpt, not full body, keeps this an order of magnitude smaller and should be the default.

title: R2 Class B ops per page view for a snapshot approaches zero at real traffic, not one, once the Worker edge-caches it
summary: A single GET against R2 is one Class B operation at 0.36 dollars per million -- negligible even uncached. But fronted by a Worker using the Cache API or a cache_ttl on the assets binding, only the first request per edge location after a change is a real R2 GET; every other view in that cache window is served from the edge with zero R2 operations. The honest number depends entirely on the assumed cache-hit ratio, which nothing in this research measured directly.

title: D1 Time Travel restores to any minute in the last 30 days on Paid, 7 days on Free -- no separate backup product needed
summary: Fetched 2026-09-04. wrangler d1 time-travel restore takes a timestamp and restores the whole database in place; restoring again to an earlier bookmark undoes a bad restore. This is D1's entire backup and point-in-time-recovery story -- there is no separate scheduled-backup feature to configure.

title: Does R2 actually support native object versioning? Cloudflare's own docs and third-party reports disagree
summary: The object-lifecycles doc (fetched 2026-09-04) covers expiration, storage-class transition, and abort-incomplete-multipart-upload rules but never mentions versioning at all. A Cloudflare Community feature request from 2023 explicitly states versioning is not a built-in R2 feature and asks for it, and no later official changelog entry found in this research confirms it shipped. Do not design a backup strategy around R2 native versioning without confirming current status directly in the dashboard -- the DIY alternative (a Worker plus event notifications plus a Queue) is what practitioners describe instead.

title: One practitioner argues for a Durable Object SQLite database per user or tenant instead of a shared D1 database, even for plain CRUD
summary: Article dated 2025-03-23, fetched 2026-09-04. The argument is architectural, not benchmarked: per-tenant isolation with no cross-contamination risk, no D1 provisioning ceremony (the first request just creates the SQLite database), and lower latency because each DO instantiates near its own users. The author names no numbers and offers personal production experience as the only evidence, which is why this is fringe rather than an established pattern -- but it is a real alternative to this research's own D1-for-identity recommendation, worth remembering if per-user isolation ever becomes a requirement.

title: Does purging a compacted R2 object or rewriting git history actually satisfy GDPR erasure once a CDN edge has already cached the old copy?
summary: Nothing found in this research, in Cloudflare's docs, or in the house's own design notes addresses cache-purge-on-erasure directly. A compaction Worker deleting an R2 object or a forced git-history rewrite removes the origin copy, but an edge cache_ttl window (or a client's own cached response) can still serve the erased content until it expires. This is a real gap in every architecture considered here, not just the event-sourced ones -- and it is the kind of question that needs a legal answer as much as a technical one.

title: Does a DO-per-topic design hit meaningful cold-start latency once thousands of topics exist? Unmeasured by Cloudflare or this research
summary: durable-objects.md documents the billing and hibernation model in detail but has no numbers for first-request latency when a DO wakes from cold, and this research found no Cloudflare-published figure either. At the scale question 6 poses (10000 topics), most objects would be cold most of the time -- worth measuring directly against a real deployment before treating one-DO-per-topic as free of a latency cost, rather than assuming it from the pricing model alone.

title: Storage cost per 1M events: DO SQLite and D1 price writes identically, but D1 charges 3.75x more per GB stored than DO SQLite
summary: Both bill 1.00 dollar per million rows written and 0.001 dollar per million rows read (D1 pricing page and DO pricing page fetched 2026-09-04, both agree). At roughly 100 bytes/event, 1M events is about 0.1GB: storage runs 0.02 dollars/month on DO SQLite (0.20/GB-mo) versus 0.075 dollars/month on D1 (0.75/GB-mo) for the same bytes -- a real, if small at this scale, difference that widens at higher volumes. R2 stores the same 0.1GB for 0.0015 dollars/month if written as one compacted object, but costs 4.50 dollars in Class A ops alone if written as 1M separate small objects instead of one batch -- batching before writing to R2 is not optional, it is a roughly 3000x cost difference.

title: D1 database size cap: 500MB free plan, 10GB Workers Paid plan, per database
summary: Fetched 2026-09-04 from D1's limits page, agreeing with the pricing page's storage-billing tiers. 50000 databases per account on Paid (10 on Free), so the cap is per-database, not per-account -- a design that shards by topic or tenant into many small databases sidesteps the single-database ceiling entirely, at the cost of cross-database queries becoming impossible.

title: Page.store() already exists in core: url-keyed local handle, get/set/patch/clear
summary: Landed 2026-08-31. Page.class.js store() returns Page.Store keyed on this.prefix plus (page.store_key or page.url) -- read directly in Page.class.js lines 543-609. This is the seam question 1 (identity) and question 7 (migration) both point at: a page url is already the id for locally-cached state, no pages table, no auto-increment id to migrate away from.

title: Curated topic content: git files stay source of truth, static read, publish is git push
summary: Following cms/thinking.md verdict: prose and page.js content are markdown/JS files beside the page they draw, written by a human or the CMS edit page over rpc:write, read by a plain static fetch with no server, cached by the browser and CDN on deploy, deleted by git rm. No database needed for this kind at any scale this site will reach.

title: User-generated content (posts, wiki edits) needs a live write path git alone cannot give a stranger
summary: A visitor cannot git push. So source of truth during editing is a database row (D1) or a Durable Object per document; write path is Worker API; read path merges the live row with any already-published static snapshot. Publish is the compaction step in question 4 -- fold accepted edits into a git-committed or R2-served static artifact on a schedule, not per edit. Delete before publish is a DELETE row; delete after publish means a revert commit, and git history keeps the old blob regardless.

title: Activity and events (chat, likes, progress) map exactly onto the stream demo already built
summary: public/imagine/stream/ is this category already working: source of truth is an append-only log (page.jsonl locally, a DO SQLite table in production), write path is one WebSocket message the DO makes durable before it broadcasts (the output gate), read path is snapshot-plus-replay-from-offset, and there is no separate cache because the DO instance is the hot copy. Delete is an appended tombstone event or storage.sql delete, bounded by 30-day PITR.

title: Derived state (levels, reputation, counts, search index) should have no source of truth of its own
summary: notes/auth section 5 already argues this for points: compute the count from likes at read time, and only materialise a cache table once a measurement demands it, rebuildable from the real rows, never itself the source. The same rule generalises to every derived number in question 1 -- a levels or reputation column is a cache with an invalidation story that is never fully correct, so treat every derived value as a query or a rebuildable index, not a write target.

title: Identity: D1 users table keyed on (provider, provider_id), session is a signed cookie, not a stored row
summary: notes/auth sections 2-3 already worked this out: GitHub OAuth avoids ever storing a password, and the session is a stateless HMAC-signed cookie (30-day, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax) verified with WebCrypto, not a sessions table looked up on every request. Revocation is one integer, users.token_epoch, bumped to invalidate every existing cookie for that user at once -- no per-request database read.

title: (A) git files plus static only: cheapest and safest, but has no live write path at all
summary: Security/privacy are trivially good (nothing to breach, nothing dynamic to exploit), backup is git history itself, migration is trivial (it is already files). Cost is zero beyond hosting. The wall: no authn, no real-time, no user write of any kind without a human or CI in the loop -- it cannot host chat, likes, or edits by a stranger. Complexity is the lowest of all five. Right architecture for question 1's curated-content row and nothing past it.

title: (C) DO-per-topic event log plus snapshot: the only one of the five with true single-writer ordering
summary: A Durable Object is single-threaded by construction, so it is a free sequencer -- the output gate makes a delta durable before the broadcast leaves, and hibernation means a page nobody is editing costs only storage. The cost is the newest, least-documented pattern of the five: Cloudflare has no published append-log-plus-snapshot recipe, so the compaction alarm and the offset-to-row-id mapping are house-built and house-tested. Real-time and integrity are its strengths; local dev parity (question 8) is weaker than the source doc claims.

title: (E) hybrid -- D1 identity/index, DOs for live rooms, R2 for logs/media, git for curated content -- is the recommended architecture
summary: Every other option forces one storage model onto data that does not need it: (A) cannot take a live write, (B) has no coordination, (C) and (D) are needless machinery for a users table. The hybrid puts each of question 1's six kinds on the backend that already matches its own shape -- git for curated content, D1 for identity plus derived indexes, a DO per active topic or room, R2 for the compacted history and any media. The cost is real: four backends means four local-dev stories and four things that can be down.

title: Event sourcing here already buys audit, replay, and a live tail, because the house built it before naming it that
summary: public/imagine/stream/ is event sourcing under a different name: page.jsonl is the event log, page.json is the projection, and Tail.js is the subscriber fan-out. The audit trail and the live multi-window sync in the demo are not hypothetical benefits of adopting event sourcing later -- they are already working and already measured at 9ms end to end.

title: What event sourcing costs here: a second thing to keep in sync (the projection) and a compaction step nobody else in the house has to write
summary: Every consumer of activity data (a topic page count, a search index) is a projection that must be rebuilt whenever the event schema changes -- there is no schema migration story for an append-only log the way there is for a D1 ALTER TABLE. stream/doc/decisions.md already chose snapshot-plus-log over one saved document specifically because two writers make the simpler shape lose data; the log is the cost paid to keep write safety, and every reader of it now needs a replay step instead of one query.

title: Where NOT to use event sourcing here: identity/session and the money ledger
summary: Session state is deliberately NOT an event log in the house design already -- notes/auth section 3 verdicts a stateless signed cookie precisely because a lookup-per-request log would cost a database read on every page view. And a ledger needs the opposite property an event log gives for free: it needs one row per balance a reconciliation query can trust today, not a replay of every transaction since account creation just to answer what a user owns right now.

title: Committing user content into the repo is right only for a compacted, low-frequency, moderated artifact -- never a live write
summary: This repo already proves the good version of this pattern: the ai/ task log is git-committed activity history, but a human runs each landing, not a visitor's browser on every keystroke. The right shape for question 4 is the same one -- a cron or Queue consumer folds a day of chat/likes into one JSON file per day, committed once via Workers Builds or one GitHub API call, comfortably inside both the 500/hour secondary limit and the repo-size guidance. Per-event commits are wrong at any traffic above a trickle.

title: The house already has a client-layer merge rule: auth may only ever add to a page, never gate its render
summary: notes/auth section 1 states the testable property directly: every page must render, and every link must work, with the API returning 500 to every request. No content() anywhere awaits the API before rendering, because capture is synchronous and async content appends into a container placed first -- so a failed fetch just means the enhancement (a like count, a signed-in name) never shows, not a broken page.

title: Recommend the client layer as the default merge point; reserve the Worker layer for auth and the /api/ prefix only
summary: Failure mode of a Worker-layer merge: if the merge logic lives inside the one script serving assets, a bug in that script can take the whole site down, not just the dynamic feature -- the opposite of the static-hosting safety question 5 is asking about. Failure mode of a client-layer merge: it degrades silently and correctly by design, per notes/auth. The Worker layer should stay narrow -- terminate /api/* and nothing else -- so a dynamic-feature bug cannot become a static-page outage.

title: Durable Objects get the same 30-day point-in-time recovery as D1, via getBookmarkForTime, for free
summary: Already cited in the house's own doc, re-verified 2026-09-04 against the live Cloudflare pricing and limits pages, which still agree on the SQLite-backed billing model. getBookmarkForTime() restores a whole DO to a moment in its last 30 days -- version history with no extra code, same window as D1's paid-tier Time Travel.

title: wrangler d1 export dumps a database to a file, but there is no d1 import -- the seed path is wrangler d1 execute --file
summary: Already established in cms/thinking.md and unchanged as of this research. Every backend in the Store seam must be able to dump itself back to plain files to avoid lock-in -- D1Store via wrangler d1 export, R2 objects by their nature already files, a DOStore via a SQL SELECT loop. If a backend cannot become a directory of files, the house rule is do not add it.

title: Migrating (C) to (E) needs one seam: a Store interface with file, D1, and DO backends behind the same calls
summary: The predecessor project (frozen-helix, read-only reference) worked through nearly this problem under the name Saver: FileSaver, then a SQLiteSaver/D1Saver, then a DOSaver, all behind one interface, with an explicit thing.migrate(targetSaver) method that is never silent or automatic. This repo's ext/Saver already has three of five methods (load/save/delete) and is missing list() and append() -- landing those two is the actual unblocking step before any backend migration is possible, not a new architecture.

title: Verified: Socket.js hardcodes the dev socket to window.location.host, exactly the line durable-objects.md says would change for a DO
summary: Read directly from public/framework/dev/Socket/Socket.js: connect() does this.ws = new WebSocket(this.protocol plus window.location.host), with no parameter or override point. Pointing a page at a per-topic DO instead of the site's own host is a real code change in exactly one place, matching the source doc's claim precisely.

title: Verified: Socket.js also hardcodes a localhost-only gate a DO-backed page would need lifted, unmentioned by the source doc
summary: initialize() only calls connect() when hostname is localhost, 127.0.0.1, or ends in .localhost; everywhere else it sets this.disabled = true and never opens a socket, by design, to keep static hosting a hard guarantee. A DO-backed live page in production needs exactly the opposite off localhost. So the change is not just swapping the URL -- it is deciding, page by page, which pages get to defeat the one gate that currently makes every socket a dev-only feature.

title: Verified: the offset is a byte position on disk, but the opaque wire shape means a row id needs no client change
summary: Server/plugins/SocketServer/Tail.js reads a subscribed .jsonl file from a byte offset that always lands just past a newline, and its resolve() function requires the path to exist under public/ on the real filesystem -- a DO has no file, so this server-side module has no DO equivalent and would be fully replaced, exactly as durable-objects.md already says. What survives unchanged is the client shape: subscribe sends [url, offset] and the push handler takes (path, lines, offset) as plain values, never interpreting the number -- so a DO emitting a row id instead of a byte count needs zero changes in Socket.js or live.js.

title: wrangler dev and node server.js are two separate local toolchains today, not one shared local-dev story
summary: Nothing in this repo currently wires the framework's own dev server (chokidar plus Tail.js, watching public/) to wrangler dev (Miniflare simulating a DO under .wrangler/state). Local dev parity as durable-objects.md frames it is really a claim about the client wire contract being transport-agnostic enough to point at either backend, which this research verified is true -- but running both together, or migrating one project between them, is still two toolchains a developer runs separately, not one.

title: A Durable Object is a free sequencer because its output gate makes a write durable before the broadcast leaves
summary: Already documented and re-verified 2026-09-04 against the live Cloudflare storage-api docs: the runtime pauses outgoing network messages from a DO until all previous writes are confirmed flushed to disk, so there is no window where a subscriber sees a delta the DO could still lose. This is single-writer-per-topic and ordering solved by the platform, not by application code.

title: A D1-only design loses serialization: two Workers can race a read-modify-write on the same row with nothing stopping them
summary: cms/thinking.md already made this argument for a single-author CMS and it generalises directly to question 9: D1 gives you SQL, not a lock. Getting single-writer behavior out of D1 alone means hand-rolling optimistic version columns or a transaction pattern D1 does not natively serialize the way one Durable Object does by construction. This is the concrete answer to what a D1-only design loses versus (C) or (E).

title: Idempotency is not optional for a compaction alarm: Cloudflare alarms retry up to 6 times, at-least-once
summary: Already documented and unchanged on re-check: a DO's alarm() handler folding the log into a snapshot must tolerate being called more than once for the same logical trigger, because the platform's own retry guarantee is at-least-once, not exactly-once. Any compaction or idempotency-key scheme in this platform's design has to assume duplicate delivery is normal, not an edge case.

title: The challenge (filesystem-first, JSONL everywhere) is right for solo-authored content, wrong past one concurrent writer at volume
summary: Every piece of this challenge already works for the site's own content and its own dev-server activity logs, at the scale of one human editing and a handful of live tabs. It stops being right the moment a stranger is writing concurrently at any real rate: git has no safe way to accept a live append from an unauthenticated browser, and a JSONL file committed forever with no rewrite grows the repo without bound -- exactly the version-churn regret the predecessor project (frozen-helix, read-only reference) never resolved by cleaning up old versions of the same file.

title: Envelope sizes measured against the house's own delta and event shapes: 94-127 bytes per line, well under any transport limit
summary: Computed 2026-09-04 using Node Buffer.byteLength against three real envelopes: the stream delta contract {at,op,path,value} measures 99 bytes for a representative set-op; a flat chat-message shape {at,user,room,text} measures 94 bytes; a like-append event measures 127 bytes. All three are far under the 2MB D1/DO row cap and the 32KiB DO WebSocket-attachment cap, so envelope size is not a binding constraint at any of the scales this research considered -- request/operation COUNT is the real cost driver, not bytes.

title: Recommendation: architecture (E), phased -- static first, D1 for identity next, a DO only when a room needs coordination
summary: Matches cms/thinking.md's already-argued sequencing and this research's findings across all nine questions: ship (A) alone first since it needs no backend at all; add D1 plus a Worker only the day a stranger must write (identity, likes); add one DO only for the first feature that genuinely needs single-writer ordering (a live room), not before. This defers R2 and event-log compaction until an actual activity feed is scoped, which the payments and realtime sibling topics should settle independently.
